To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the Internet is not a panacea for democracy; (2) it is a powerful tool, but only if used wisely; and (3) the Internet is best used as a tool for democracy in the hands of citizens, not governments.

1) GOLD is a promising approach to enhancing the quality of administrative rulemaking; 2) GOLD is an approach to rulemaking that is consistent with the values and principles of EPG; 3) EPG advocates and GOLD proponents should work more closely together to advance the goals of both approaches; 4) GOLD is a useful way to advance the EPG agenda, and EPG is a useful way for GOLD to advance its own goals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how to make the most of the potential of ICTs to enhance democratic participation.
the question of how we can create more democratic and participatory institutions that are also more efficient and effective.
the question of how the Internet can best be used to facilitate the creation of new forms of democratic participation and governance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the GOLD model is not a perfect fit for the EPG model, but it is close enough to be a useful starting point.

EPG is a promising and useful model for thinking about the future of democratic experimentalism, and that the authors' and others' insights into the nature and design of such experiments are highly pertinent to the future of GOLD and other initiatives in cyberdemocracy.
GOLD is a necessary but not sufficient component of EPG.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
EPG is a model of participatory governance in which citizens and public officials are empowered to work together to identify problems and develop solutions that are both effective and democratic.
we have been able to demonstrate the feasibility of a participatory approach to rulemaking, but that we have not yet been able to demonstrate its efficacy in terms of the rulemaking process itself.
EPG is a promising model for the future of governance, and GOLD is a promising way of achieving EPG's aims.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the most promising approach to strengthening democracy is to combine the two approaches to institutional innovation.
we need to think more deeply about the ways in which new information and communications technologies can be harnessed to achieve the goals of empowered participatory governance.
the EPG model can be applied to a wide array of governance problems and that there are many different ways in which EPG institutions can be constructed.
